concepts: Sum of a G.P. and of its odd-placed terms
questions.question: If in a G.P. of $64$ terms, the sum of all the terms is $7$ times the sum of the odd terms of the G.P., then the common ratio of the G.P. is equal to :
questions.key_idea: The odd-placed terms form a G.P. with ratio $r^2$, so both sums carry the factor $1-r^{64}$ and it cancels.
solution: All terms: a G.P. of $64$ terms with ratio $r$, so the sum is $\frac{a(1-r^{64})}{1-r}$.
Odd-placed terms: $32$ terms with ratio $r^2$, so the sum is $\frac{a(1-r^{64})}{1-r^2}$.
Cancel $a(1-r^{64})$ (non-zero, else every sum is $0$): $\frac{1}{1-r}=\frac{7}{(1-r)(1+r)}$, so $1+r=7$.
questions.correction_note: PDF jumps from the two sum formulas straight to 'r = 6' without showing the cancellation of a(1-r^64) or the step 1+r=7 (and that the sum of odd terms is a 32-term G.P. with ratio r^2). These steps were added; the answer (B) 6 is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Each even-placed term is $r$ times the odd-placed term just before it, so $S_{even}=r\,S_{odd}$.
solution: Every even-placed term equals $r$ times its odd-placed partner, so $S_{even}=r\,S_{odd}$.

useful_results: For a G.P. with an even number of terms, $S_{even}=r\,S_{odd}$, so $S=(1+r)S_{odd}$; the ratio $S/S_{odd}=1+r$ is independent of the first term and of the number of terms.
Odd-placed terms of a G.P. $(a,ar,ar^2,\dots)$ form a G.P. with first term $a$ and ratio $r^2$; even-placed terms form one with first term $ar$ and ratio $r^2$.

concepts: Characteristic polynomial and Cayley–Hamilton theorem
questions.question: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&a&0\\1&3&1\\0&5&b\end{pmatrix}$. If $A^3=4A^2-A-21I$, where $I$ is the identity matrix of order $3\times3$, then $2a+3b$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $A$ satisfies $\lambda^3-4\lambda^2+\lambda+21=0$, so match it with the characteristic polynomial of $A$.
solution: The characteristic equation of $A$ is $|A-\lambda I|=0$: $\begin{vmatrix}2-\lambda&a&0\\1&3-\lambda&1\\0&5&b-\lambda\end{vmatrix}=0$.
The given relation is $A^3-4A^2+A+21I=0$, i.e. $-\lambda^3+4\lambda^2-\lambda-21=0$ is the same polynomial.
Check the constant term: $6b-10-ab=-6-10-5=-21$, as required.
questions.correction_note: PDF's working is right but incomplete: it never checks the constant term (6b-10-ab = -21) and does not justify identifying the given cubic with the characteristic polynomial. Added the constant-term check; verified with sympy that a=-5, b=-1 is the only solution of A^3-4A^2+A+21I=0, so the identification is safe. Answer (B) -13 unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Compare only the invariants: $\operatorname{tr}A=4$ and $\det A=-21$ for the cubic $\lambda^3-4\lambda^2+\lambda+21$.
solution: The characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^3-(\operatorname{tr}A)\lambda^2+(\dots)\lambda-\det A$, and it equals $\lambda^3-4\lambda^2+\lambda+21$.
Expand $\det A$ along the first row: $2(3b-5)-a(b-0)=6b-10-ab$.
$2a+3b=-10-3=-13$ (the same answer, with no need to expand the full characteristic polynomial).

useful_results: If a monic cubic $p$ satisfies $p(A)=0$ for a $3\times3$ matrix whose minimal polynomial has degree $3$, then $p$ is the characteristic polynomial; read off $\operatorname{tr}A=-(\text{coeff of }\lambda^2)$ and $\det A=-(\text{constant term})$.
For $3\times3$: $\chi_A(\lambda)=\lambda^3-(\operatorname{tr}A)\lambda^2+(\text{sum of principal }2\times2\text{ minors})\lambda-\det A$.
Instance: $\operatorname{tr}A=5+b=4$ and $\det A=6b-10-ab=-21$ give $(a,b)=(-5,-1)$.

concepts: Adjoint and trace of a diagonal matrix
Sum of sines of angles in A.P. (trigonometric identity)
questions.question:
Let $R= egin{pmatrix}x&0&0\0&y&0\0&0&z\end{pmatrix}$ be a non-zero $3	imes3$ matrix, where $x\sin	heta=y\sin\left(	heta+ rac{2\pi}{3}ight)=z\sin\left(	heta+ rac{4\pi}{3}ight)
eq0$, $	heta\in(0,2\pi)$. For a square matrix $M$, let $\operatorname{trace}(M)$ denote the sum of all diagonal entries of $M$. Then, among the statements :
(I) $\operatorname{Trace}(R)=0$
(II) If $\operatorname{trace}(\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}(R)))=0$, then $R$ has exactly one non-zero entry.
questions.answer: (B) Only (II) is true  [PDF key: (D); see note]
questions.key_idea: $\sum\sin\left(\theta+\frac{2k\pi}{3}\right)=0$ gives $\frac1x+\frac1y+\frac1z=0$, so $xy+yz+zx=0$ and then $\operatorname{trace}R\neq0$.
solution: Since the common value is non-zero, $x\sin\theta\neq0$ etc., so $x,y,z\neq0$ (all three diagonal entries are non-zero).

Let the common value be $c\neq0$: $\sin\theta=\frac cx$, $\sin\left(\theta+\frac{2\pi}3\right)=\frac cy$, $\sin\left(\theta+\frac{4\pi}3\right)=\frac cz$. Adding: $\frac1x+\frac1y+\frac1z=0$, so $xy+yz+zx=0$.

(I) $\operatorname{Trace}(R)=x+y+z$. If $x+y+z=0$ together with $xy+yz+zx=0$, then $x^2+y^2+z^2=(x+y+z)^2-2(xy+yz+zx)=0$, so $x=y=z=0$, contradicting $x,y,z\neq0$. Hence $\operatorname{Trace}(R)\neq0$ and (I) is false.
So $\operatorname{trace}(\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}R))=xyz\,(x+y+z)$, and this is never $0$ because $x,y,z\neq0$ and $x+y+z\neq0$.
The hypothesis of (II) can therefore never hold, so the implication in (II) is vacuously true (R always has three non-zero entries, but the 'if' part is never met).
Hence only (II) is true: option (B). (The PDF stops at 'trace $\neq0$' and calls (II) false, key (D).)
questions.correction_note: PDF says statement (II) is false (key D). But the PDF itself shows trace(adj(adj R)) = xyz(x+y+z) is never 0, so the 'if' part of (II) is never satisfied and the conditional is vacuously TRUE; strictly the answer is (B) Only (II) is true. The PDF/official-style key (D) treats (II) as false because its conclusion ('exactly one non-zero entry') is impossible. Needs the user's decision on which reading to teach.

alternate_solutions.idea: Because $e_2=xy+yz+zx=0$, the identity $x^2+y^2+z^2=(x+y+z)^2$ gives $|\operatorname{trace}R|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}>0$.
solution: The condition 'trace $=0$' in (II) is impossible, so (II) is true only vacuously: answer (B) (the same answer as the main solution).

useful_results: $\sin\theta+\sin\left(\theta+\frac{2\pi}3\right)+\sin\left(\theta+\frac{4\pi}3\right)=0$ for every $\theta$; likewise for cosines (cube roots of unity phasors sum to $0$).
For an $n\times n$ matrix: $\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)=|A|^{n-2}A$ and $|\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^{n-1}$.
If $e_1=x+y+z$ and $e_2=xy+yz+zx=0$ for reals, then $e_1^2=x^2+y^2+z^2$, so $e_1=0\iff x=y=z=0$.
A conditional 'if $P$ then $Q$' with $P$ never true is vacuously true; check whether the hypothesis can occur before judging such statements.

concepts: Properties of the adjoint and the inverse of a matrix
questions.question: If $A$, $B$, and $\left(\operatorname{adj}(A^{-1})+\operatorname{adj}(B^{-1})\right)$ are non-singular matrices of the same order, then the inverse of $A\left(\operatorname{adj}(A^{-1})+\operatorname{adj}(B^{-1})\right)^{-1}B$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $(XYZ)^{-1}=Z^{-1}Y^{-1}X^{-1}$, and $\operatorname{adj}(A^{-1})=\frac{A}{|A|}$ turns the middle factor into $\frac A{|A|}+\frac B{|B|}$.
solution: Reverse the order of the product: $=B^{-1}\left(\operatorname{adj}(A^{-1})+\operatorname{adj}(B^{-1})\right)A^{-1}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Test with scalar matrices of order $2$: $A=2I$, $B=I$, and eliminate the options.
solution: Take order $2$ with $A=2I$, $B=I$; then $A^{-1}=\frac12I$ and for $2\times2$ matrices $\operatorname{adj}(kI)=kI$.
$\operatorname{adj}(A^{-1})=\frac12I$, $\operatorname{adj}(B^{-1})=I$, so the sum is $\frac32I$ and its inverse is $\frac23I$.
The matrix is $A\cdot\frac23I\cdot B=2I\cdot\frac23\cdot I=\frac43I$, so its inverse is $\frac34I$.

useful_results: $\operatorname{adj}(A^{-1})=(\operatorname{adj}A)^{-1}=\frac{A}{|A|}$ and $\operatorname{adj}A=|A|A^{-1}$ (valid for invertible $A$).
$(XYZ)^{-1}=Z^{-1}Y^{-1}X^{-1}$; $\operatorname{adj}(XY)=\operatorname{adj}Y\,\operatorname{adj}X$.
Substituting simple scalar or diagonal matrices is a fast way to test or eliminate options in identity-type matrix questions (check on one numerical case that exactly one option survives).

concepts: Arithmetic progression and geometric progression combined
questions.question: Let $3,a,b,c$ be in A.P. and $3,a-1,b+1,c+9$ be in G.P. Then, the arithmetic mean of $a$, $b$ and $c$ is :
questions.key_idea: A.P. gives $b=2a-3$; the G.P. gives $(a-1)^2=3(b+1)$, a quadratic in $a$ with one rejected root.
solution: $(a-1)(a-7)=0$; $a=7$ since $a\neq1$ ($a-1$ is a term of a G.P. with first term $3$, so it is non-zero).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the common difference $d$: the G.P. ratio comes out as $2$ at once, and the mean of three A.P. terms is the middle term $b$.
solution: Then $a=7$, $b=11$, $c=15$; check the G.P.: $3,6,12,24$ with ratio $2$. ✓.
The mean of the three equally spaced terms $a,b,c$ is the middle term $b=11$ (the same answer).

useful_results: Three equally spaced numbers $a,b,c$ (A.P.) have mean equal to the middle one, $b$.
If $3,a,b,c$ is an A.P. with difference $d$, then $b+1=2(a-1)$ whenever $d$ makes $b=2a-3$; spotting a doubling relation between the G.P. terms gives the common ratio quickly.
Combined A.P./G.P. questions: express everything through one variable ($d$ or $a$), get a quadratic, and discard the root that makes a G.P. term zero.

concepts: Properties of determinants: $|kA|=k^n|A|$
Integer solutions of $\alpha^2-\beta^2=n$
questions.question: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&\alpha&\beta\\0&\beta&\alpha\end{pmatrix}$ and $|2A|^3=2^{21}$ where $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb Z$. Then a value of $\alpha$ is :
questions.key_idea: $|2A|^3=2^9|A|^3$ gives $|A|=16$, so $\alpha^2-\beta^2=16$ in integers.
solution: Integer solutions: $(\alpha-\beta)(\alpha+\beta)=16$ with both factors of the same parity gives $\alpha=\pm5,\beta=\pm3$ or $\alpha=\pm4,\beta=0$.
Among the options only $\alpha=5$ occurs ($17,3,9$ give $\alpha^2-16=273,-7,65$, none a perfect square), with $\beta=\pm3$.
questions.correction_note: PDF writes '(alpha, beta) = (5, 3)' directly after alpha^2 - beta^2 = 16 without showing that integers satisfy it or why the other options fail. Added the factor-pair enumeration and the option check. Answer (A) 5 unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Factor-pair parity: $(\alpha-\beta)(\alpha+\beta)=16$ with both factors even lists all integer values of $\alpha$ at once.
solution: $\alpha-\beta$ and $\alpha+\beta$ have the same parity and their product is even, so both are even: write them as $2u,2v$ with $uv=4$.
The only listed option among $\{\pm4,\pm5\}$ is $5$ (the same answer).

useful_results: $|kA|=k^n|A|$ for an $n\times n$ matrix, so $|2A|^3=2^{3n}|A|^3$; for $n=3$ this is $2^9|A|^3$.
The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\beta\\\beta&\alpha\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $(\alpha-\beta)(\alpha+\beta)$ and eigenvalues $\alpha\pm\beta$.
$m^2-n^2=N$ in integers: $m-n$ and $m+n$ must have the same parity, so an odd $N$ needs odd factors and $N\equiv2\pmod4$ has no solution.

concepts: Infinitely many solutions of a system of linear equations
Distance of a point from a line (circle touching a line)
questions.question: Let the system of equations $2x+3y+5z=9$, $7x+3y-2z=8$, $12x+3y-(4+\lambda)z=16-\mu$ have infinitely many solutions. Then the radius of the circle centred at $(\lambda,\mu)$ and touching the line $4x=3y$ is :
questions.key_idea: Infinitely many solutions need $D=0$ and $D_x=0$; the radius is the perpendicular distance from the centre to the line.
solution: The circle touches $4x-3y=0$, so its radius is the distance from the centre: $r=\frac{|4(5)-3(9)|}{\sqrt{4^2+3^2}}$.
questions.correction_note: PDF's determinant D shows the second row as (4, 3, -2); the system's second equation is 7x+3y-2z=8, so the row must be (7, 3, -2). With 4 the PDF's D would give lambda = 26, not 5. With the correct row 7 (as used in the printed question) lambda = 5. Corrected; answer (D) unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Infinitely many solutions means the third equation is a combination $pE_1+qE_2$ of the first two; match coefficients.
solution: Write $E_3=pE_1+qE_2$ (valid since $E_1,E_2$ are not proportional and the system is dependent).
Centre $(5,9)$ and distance to $4x-3y=0$: $\frac{|20-27|}5=\frac75$ (the same answer).

alternate_solutions.idea: Solve $x,y$ in terms of $z$ from the first two equations and demand the third holds for all $z$.
solution: From $2x+3y=9-5z$ and $7x+3y=8+2z$: subtract to get $5x=7z-1$, so $x=\frac{7z-1}{5}$.
This must hold for all $z$ (one-parameter family): $\lambda=5$ and $\mu=9$, so the centre is $(5,9)$ and $r=\frac75$.

useful_results: A $3\times3$ system has infinitely many solutions iff its rows are dependent in the augmented matrix (rank of coefficient matrix = rank of augmented matrix $<3$); $D=0$ alone is not enough, so check one $D_i=0$ or a combination of rows.
Distance from $(x_0,y_0)$ to $ax+by+c=0$ is $\frac{|ax_0+by_0+c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$; a circle touching the line has this as its radius.
Instance: $E_3=-E_1+2E_2$ gives $\lambda=5,\ \mu=9$; $r=\frac75$.

concepts: Infinitely many solutions of a linear system
Integer solutions of a parametric family of solutions
questions.question: Let the system of equations $x+5y-z=1$, $4x+3y-3z=7$, $24x+y+\lambda z=\mu$, $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R$, have infinitely many solutions. Then the number of the solutions of this system, if $x,y,z$ are integers and satisfy $7\le x+y+z\le77$, is :
questions.key_idea: The solutions form a line: put $z=k$, solve for $x,y$, and integrality forces $k\equiv3\pmod{17}$.
solution: $x+5y-z=1$ ... (1); $4x+3y-3z=7$ ... (2); $24x+y+\lambda z=\mu$ ... (3). Infinitely many solutions exist for suitable $\lambda,\mu$ ($\lambda=-17,\mu=45$), so the solutions are the line common to (1) and (2).
For $y$ to be an integer, $k=3+17t$; then $x=\frac{32+12(3+17t)}{17}=4+12t$ is also an integer.
questions.correction_note: PDF ends at 'k = 3, 20, 37' with no reason why only those k give integers (k = 3 mod 17) and does not state the count; also it does not show that lambda, mu exist (lambda = -17, mu = 45). Added the integrality step, the three solutions and the count. Verified by brute force: exactly 3 integer points. Answer (B) 3 unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: The solution set is a line through an integer point with a primitive direction vector $=$ cross product of the two normals.
solution: The direction of the line of intersection of planes (1),(2) is $(1,5,-1)\times(4,3,-3)=(-12,-1,-17)$, i.e. $\pm(12,1,17)$ (components have gcd $1$).
A particular integer point: $(4,0,3)$ satisfies (1): $4+0-3=1$ and (2): $16-9=7$.
Since the direction vector is primitive, all integer points of the line are $(4,0,3)+t(12,1,17)$, $t\in\mathbb Z$.
Hence there are $3$ solutions (the same answer).

useful_results: If a $3\times3$ system has a line of solutions, the direction vector is the cross product of two independent coefficient rows; integer points on the line are $P_0+t\,\mathbf d$ with $\mathbf d$ the primitive integer direction.
To count integer points on a line with a linear constraint, parametrise by $t\in\mathbb Z$ and express the constraint as a range of $t$.
Instance: $x+y+z=7+30t$, so $7\le x+y+z\le77$ gives $t=0,1,2$.

concepts: Determinant of the adjoint of a matrix: $|\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}(kA))|$
questions.question: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&2+p&2+p+q\\4&6+2p&8+3p+2q\\6&12+3p&20+6p+3q\end{pmatrix}$. If $\det(\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}(3A)))=2^m\cdot3^n$, $m,n\in\mathbb N$, then $m+n$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Row operations show $|A|=8$ for all $p,q$; then $|\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}M)|=|M|^{(n-1)^2}=|M|^4$ with $M=3A$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The answer must not depend on $p,q$, so set $p=q=0$ to evaluate $|A|$ at once.
solution: The problem assumes $m,n$ are fixed, so $|A|$ is the same for all $p,q$; take $p=q=0$.

useful_results: For an $n\times n$ matrix: $\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}M)=|M|^{n-2}M$ and $|\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}M)|=|M|^{(n-1)^2}$.
When a determinant is claimed to be independent of parameters, substituting convenient values ($p=q=0$) gives it instantly; confirm with one row-reduction.

concepts: Method of differences: telescoping sum of an infinite series
questions.question: If $\sum_{r=1}^{n}T_r=\frac{(2n-1)(2n+1)(2n+3)(2n+5)}{64}$, then $\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac1{T_r}\right)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $T_n=S_n-S_{n-1}$ factorises to $\frac{(2n-1)(2n+1)(2n+3)}8$, and $\frac1{T_n}$ splits into a telescoping difference.
solution: As $n\to\infty$ the last term tends to $0$, so the limit is $\frac23$.

(Remark: the formula for $T_n$ holds for $n\ge2$; at $n=1$ the printed $S_n$ gives $S_1=\frac{105}{64}$ but the formula gives $\frac{15}8$ because $S_0$ would be $-\frac{15}{64}$, not $0$. The intended answer, taking the formula for all $n\ge1$, is $\frac23$.)
questions.correction_note: PDF's telescoping line labels the second factor wrongly: it shows 1/((2n-1)(2n+1)) - 1/((2n-1)(2n+3)) and S_n = 2(1/(1.3) - 1/((2n-1)(2n+3))); the correct difference is 1/((2n-1)(2n+1)) - 1/((2n+1)(2n+3)) and S_n = 2(1/3 - 1/((2n+1)(2n+3))). Also the question itself is slightly inconsistent: with the printed S_n, S_0 = -15/64 != 0, so T_1 = S_1 = 105/64 differs from the formula value 15/8; strictly the limit would be 64/105 + 2/15 = 26/35, which is not an option. The intended key (C) 2/3 (formula for all n) is kept.

alternate_solutions.idea: Partial fractions: $\frac{8}{(2n-1)(2n+1)(2n+3)}=\frac1{2n-1}-\frac2{2n+1}+\frac1{2n+3}$, which telescopes in two strands.
solution: As $N\to\infty$ this tends to $1-\frac13=\frac23$ (the same answer).

useful_results: If $\sum_{r\le n}T_r=S_n$ is given, then $T_n=S_n-S_{n-1}$ for $n\ge2$ (and $T_1=S_1$); check that the formula for $T_n$ also fits $n=1$.
$\frac1{(2n-1)(2n+1)(2n+3)}=\frac14\left[\frac1{(2n-1)(2n+1)}-\frac1{(2n+1)(2n+3)}\right]$; in general $\frac1{n(n+1)\cdots(n+k)}=\frac1k\left[\frac1{n\cdots(n+k-1)}-\frac1{(n+1)\cdots(n+k)}\right]$.
Instance: $\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{8}{(2r-1)(2r+1)(2r+3)}=\frac23$.

concepts: Infinitely many solutions of a linear system
Integer solutions of a parametric family of solutions
questions.question: Let the system of equations $x+5y-z=1$, $4x+3y-3z=7$, $24x+y+\lambda z=\mu$, $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R$, have infinitely many solutions. Then the number of the solutions of this system, if $x,y,z$ are integers and satisfy $7\le x+y+z\le77$, is :
questions.key_idea: The solutions form a line: put $z=k$, solve for $x,y$, and integrality forces $k\equiv3\pmod{17}$.
solution: $x+5y-z=1$ ... (1); $4x+3y-3z=7$ ... (2); $24x+y+\lambda z=\mu$ ... (3). Infinitely many solutions exist for suitable $\lambda,\mu$ ($\lambda=-17,\mu=45$), so the solutions are the line common to (1) and (2).
For $x,y,z$ to be integers, $17\mid(k-3)$, i.e. $k=3+17t$; then $x=4+12t$ is an integer too.
questions.correction_note: Duplicate of Q8 (printed Q68 = Q71). PDF ends at 'k = 3, 20, 37' with no reason why only those k give integers and no count; also does not show lambda, mu exist (lambda = -17, mu = 45). Added the integrality step, the three solutions and the count. Brute force confirms exactly 3. Answer (B) 3 unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Treat $s=x+y+z$ as a third equation and solve for $x,y,z$ in terms of $s$; integrality then needs $s\equiv7\pmod{30}$.
solution: Add $x+y+z=s$ to (1),(2); the coefficient determinant is $\begin{vmatrix}1&5&-1\\4&3&-3\\1&1&1\end{vmatrix}=-30\neq0$, so the solution is unique for each $s$.
Integers: $y\in\mathbb Z$, so $s=7+30y$ and then $x,z$ are integers automatically.

useful_results: For a consistent system of rank $2$ in three unknowns, the solutions form a line $P_0+t\mathbf d$; adding the constraint expression as an extra equation gives the parameter in terms of that expression.
To count integer solutions subject to a linear bound, convert integrality into a congruence on the free parameter ($k\equiv3\pmod{17}$) before counting.
Instance: $x+y+z=7+30t$ for $t=0,1,2$ within $[7,77]$.

concepts: Infinitely many solutions of a linear system (Δ=0 and consistency)
questions.question: If the system of linear equations $3x+y+\beta z=3$, $2x+\alpha y-z=-3$, $x+2y+z=4$ has infinitely many solutions, then the value of $22\beta-9\alpha$ is :
questions.key_idea: Infinitely many solutions need $\Delta=0$ and $\Delta_3=0$; $\Delta_3$ is free of $\beta$ and fixes $\alpha$ first.
solution: For infinitely many solutions, $\Delta=0$ and all $\Delta_i=0$.
questions.correction_note: PDF gives alpha and beta without showing the beta calculation and does not note that rank 2 (columns 1,2 independent) makes Delta = 0 and Delta_3 = 0 sufficient for consistency. Added the beta calculation and the consistency remark; checked with sympy that at alpha = -19/9, beta = 6/11 both coefficient and augmented ranks are 2. Answer (A) 31 unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Infinite solutions mean a combination $\lambda_1E_1+\lambda_2E_2+\lambda_3E_3\equiv0$ of the equations (including the right sides); find the multipliers first.
solution: The $x$-column: $3\lambda_1+2\lambda_2+\lambda_3=0$; the right-hand column: $3\lambda_1-3\lambda_2+4\lambda_3=0$. Eliminate $\lambda_3=-3\lambda_1-2\lambda_2$ to get $-9\lambda_1-11\lambda_2=0$.

useful_results: A linear system has infinitely many solutions iff some non-trivial combination of the equations is $0=0$ (rows dependent including the constant column) and the coefficient rank is less than the number of unknowns.
For $3\times3$ systems with $\Delta=0$: if two columns of the coefficient matrix are independent, then $\Delta_i=0$ for the third column is enough for consistency.
Instance: $-11E_1+9E_2+15E_3=0$ with $\alpha=-\frac{19}9,\beta=\frac6{11}$.

concepts: Infinitely many solutions of a system of linear equations
Distance of a point from a line (circle touching a line)
questions.question: Let the system of equations $2x+3y+5z=9$, $7x+3y-2z=8$, $12x+3y-(4+\lambda)z=16-\mu$ have infinitely many solutions. Then the radius of the circle centred at $(\lambda,\mu)$ and touching the line $4x=3y$ is :
questions.key_idea: Infinitely many solutions need $D=0$ and $D_x=0$; the radius is the perpendicular distance from the centre to the line.
solution: The radius is the distance from $(5,9)$ to $4x-3y=0$: $r=\frac{|4(5)-3(9)|}{\sqrt{4^2+3^2}}$.
questions.correction_note: Duplicate of Q7 (printed Q67 = Q73). PDF's determinant D shows the second row as (4, 3, -2) instead of (7, 3, -2); with 4 it would give lambda = 26. Corrected to 7 (lambda = 5). Answer (D) unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Solve $x,y$ in terms of $z$ from the first two equations and demand the third equation hold for every $z$.
solution: From the first two: subtract to get $5x=7z-1$, so $x=\frac{7z-1}5$, and $y=\frac{9-5z-2x}{3}=\frac{47-39z}{15}$.

useful_results: A dependent system is a one-parameter family in $z$: the third equation must hold identically in $z$, so the coefficient of $z$ and the constant must both match.
Radius of a circle centre $(h,k)$ touching $ax+by+c=0$: $\frac{|ah+bk+c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$.
Instance: $(5-\lambda)z+7=16-\mu$ gives $(\lambda,\mu)=(5,9)$.

concepts: Matrices with $A^2=I$: eigenvalues of $A=I-2MM^T$
questions.question: Let $A=I_2-2MM^T$, where $M$ is a real matrix of order $2\times1$ such that $M^TM=I_1$. If $\lambda$ is a real number such that $AX=\lambda X$ holds for some non-zero real matrix $X$ of order $2\times1$, then the sum of squares of all possible values of $\lambda$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $M^TM=1$ makes $A^2=I$, so every eigenvalue satisfies $\lambda^2=1$.
solution: Both values occur: $AM=M-2M(M^TM)=-M$ gives $\lambda=-1$, and any $X\perp M$ ($M^TX=0$) gives $AX=X$, i.e. $\lambda=1$.
Sum of squares of all possible values $=1^2+(-1)^2=2$.
questions.correction_note: PDF stops at lambda = +-1 and does not show that both values are actually attained (needed for 'all possible values'). Added AM = -M and AX = X for X orthogonal to M. Answer 2 unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $M=(p,q)^T$ with $p^2+q^2=1$ and read the eigenvalues from the trace and determinant.
solution: Characteristic equation: $\lambda^2-0\cdot\lambda-1=0$, so $\lambda=\pm1$ (both attained, as both roots are real).

useful_results: $I-2uu^T$ with $u^Tu=1$ is a Householder reflection: symmetric, orthogonal, $A^2=I$, eigenvalue $-1$ (along $u$) and $+1$ (perpendicular to $u$); trace $=n-2$, $\det=-1$.
If $A^2=I$ then every eigenvalue is $\pm1$; to claim a value is 'possible' check that it is attained.
Instance: for $2\times2$: $\operatorname{tr}A=0$, $\det A=-1$, eigenvalues $\pm1$.

concepts: Solving a $2\times2$ system by Cramer's rule with sign conditions
Definite integral of a linear function
questions.question: Consider the matrices $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&-5\\3&m\end{pmatrix}$, $B=\begin{pmatrix}20\\m\end{pmatrix}$ and $X=\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}$. Let the set of all $m$, for which the system of equations $AX=B$ has a negative solution (i.e., $x<0$ and $y<0$), be the interval $(a,b)$. Then $8\int_a^b|A|\,dm$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: Solve for $x,y$ in terms of $m$; both negative gives $m\in\left(-\frac{15}2,0\right)$, where $|A|=2m+15>0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Eliminate $m$ instead: $m=\frac{3x}{1-y}$, so with $y<0$ the sign of $x$ gives the sign of $m$; and the integral is the area of a triangle.
solution: With $y<0$ we have $1-y>0$. $x<0$ needs $y<-4$, and then $m=\frac{15}{2}\cdot\frac{4+y}{1-y}$.
$g(y)=\frac{4+y}{1-y}=-1+\frac5{1-y}$ is increasing on $(-\infty,-4)$ from $-1$ (as $y\to-\infty$) to $0$ (at $y=-4$), so $m\in\left(-\frac{15}2,0\right)$.
$|A|=2m+15$ is a straight line from $0$ at $m=-\frac{15}2$ to $15$ at $m=0$: the area under it is the triangle $\frac12\cdot\frac{15}2\cdot15=\frac{225}4$.

useful_results: For $AX=B$ with $|A|\neq0$: $x=\frac{D_x}{|A|}$, $y=\frac{D_y}{|A|}$; sign conditions become sign-of-ratio inequalities solved with a number line (do not multiply by $|A|$ without its sign).
the integral of the absolute value of a linear function over an interval where it keeps one sign equals the area of a triangle/trapezium under the line, which avoids antiderivatives.
Instance: $|A|=2m+15$ on $\left(-\frac{15}2,0\right)$: area $\frac{225}4$.

concepts: Method of differences with the factorisation $1+4r^4=(2r^2-2r+1)(2r^2+2r+1)$
questions.question: If the sum of the first $10$ terms of the series $\frac{4\cdot1}{1+4\cdot1^4}+\frac{4\cdot2}{1+4\cdot2^4}+\frac{4\cdot3}{1+4\cdot3^4}+\dots$ is $\frac mn$, where $\gcd(m,n)=1$, then $m+n$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $1+4r^4=(2r^2+1)^2-(2r)^2$ factorises, and the factors differ by $4r$, so $T_r$ telescopes.
useful_results: Sophie Germain identity: $a^4+4b^4=(a^2+2b^2+2ab)(a^2+2b^2-2ab)$; here $1+4r^4=(2r^2+2r+1)(2r^2-2r+1)$. Recognise $1+4(\text{fourth power})$ at once.
When the numerator equals the difference of the two factors, $\frac{N}{PQ}=\frac1P-\frac1Q$ and the series telescopes: $\sum_{r=1}^n\frac{4r}{1+4r^4}=1-\frac1{2n^2+2n+1}$.

concepts: Skew-symmetric matrices and determinant of the adjoint of $2(A+I)$
questions.question: Let $A$ be a $3\times3$ matrix such that $X^TAX=O$ for all non-zero $3\times1$ matrices $X=\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}$. If $A\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\4\\-5\end{pmatrix}$, $A\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\4\\-8\end{pmatrix}$, and $\det(\operatorname{adj}(2(A+I)))=2^\alpha3^\beta5^\gamma$, $\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in\mathbb N$, then $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: $X^TAX=0$ for all $X$ forces $a_{ii}=0$ and $a_{ij}+a_{ji}=0$, so $A$ is skew-symmetric with three unknowns.
solution: Solving $x+y=1$ and $2x+y=0$: $x=-1$, $y=2$; then $z=4+x=3$ (all six equations check).
questions.correction_note: PDF's matrix 2(A+I) has third row (-2, -6, 2); correct is (-4, -6, 2) (twice the third row of A+I = (-2,-3,1)). It also writes '2(A+I) = 120' meaning the determinant and omits the determinant expansion det(A+I) = 15 and the adjoint rule |adj B| = |B|^2. Added these; final 44 unchanged (det(2(A+I)) = 120 verified).

alternate_solutions.idea: For a real skew-symmetric $3\times3$ matrix, $\det(I+A)=1+x^2+y^2+z^2$, so the determinant needs no expansion.
solution: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&x&y\\-x&0&z\\-y&-z&0\end{pmatrix}$ the eigenvalues are $0,\pm i\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}$, so $\det(I+A)=1\cdot(1+is)(1-is)=1+s^2$ with $s^2=x^2+y^2+z^2$.

useful_results: $X^TAX=0$ for all $X$ $\iff$ $A$ is skew-symmetric ($A^T=-A$); for a skew-symmetric $3\times3$ matrix $A$ and any $X$, $AX=\omega\times X$ with $\omega=(-z,y,-x)$.
For skew-symmetric $3\times3$: $\det A=0$ and $\det(I+A)=1+x^2+y^2+z^2$ (check: $A$ above gives $15$).
For $n\times n$: $|kA|=k^n|A|$ and $|\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^{n-1}$, so $|\operatorname{adj}(2B)|=(2^n|B|)^{n-1}$.

concepts: Sums of powers of natural numbers and the $n$th term of a quadratic sequence
questions.question: Let $\alpha=1^2+4^2+8^2+13^2+19^2+26^2+\dots$ up to $10$ terms and $\beta=\sum_{n=1}^{10}n^4$. If $4\alpha-\beta=55k+40$, then $k$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The terms $1,4,8,13,\dots$ have constant second difference, so $t_n=\frac{n^2+3n-2}{2}$; then $4\alpha-\beta$ drops to a cubic sum.
solution: Terms before squaring: $1,4,8,13,19,26,\dots$ (second differences are constant), so $t_n=an^2+bn+c$.
questions.correction_note: PDF ends '= 55(353) + 40' without evaluating the sums, so the value 353 is never derived. Added the evaluation of the cubic sum (19455) and the solve for k. Answer 353 unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $4\alpha-\beta=\sum(2t_n-n^2)(2t_n+n^2)$ (difference of squares) and factor the summand.

useful_results: If the second differences of a sequence are constant, $t_n$ is quadratic: fit $an^2+bn+c$ with three terms, or use $t_n=t_1+(n-1)\Delta_1+\binom{n-1}2\Delta_2$ with $\Delta_1=3,\Delta_2=1$ here.

concepts: Condition for no solution of a $3\times3$ linear system
questions.question: Let $S$ be the set of values of $\lambda$, for which the system of equations $6\lambda x-3y+3z=4\lambda^2$, $2x+6\lambda y+4z=1$, $3x+2y+3\lambda z=\lambda$ has no solution. Then $12\sum_{\lambda\in S}|\lambda|$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: No solution needs $D=0$ and inconsistency; $D=12(9\lambda^3-7\lambda-2)=12(\lambda-1)(3\lambda+1)(3\lambda+2)$.
solution: For no solution, $D=0$ (and the system must be inconsistent).
Check each root for inconsistency: at $\lambda=1$, the combination $2E_1+3E_2-6E_3$ kills the left side but gives $8+3-6=5\neq0$ on the right: no solution.
At $\lambda=-\frac13$: $2E_1-E_2+2E_3$ kills the left side, but the right side is $-\frac79\neq0$: no solution.
At $\lambda=-\frac23$: $16E_1-E_2+22E_3$ kills the left side, but the right side is $\frac{115}9\neq0$: no solution.
questions.correction_note: PDF stops at D = 0 and sums |lambda| over all three roots without checking that each gives NO solution (D = 0 only allows none OR infinitely many). Added the check with a left-null combination of equations for each root (ranks 2 vs 3 verified by sympy): all three give no solution. Answer 24 unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Compute $\operatorname{adj}(M)\mathbf b$ (the Cramer numerators): no solution iff $D=0$ and some numerator is non-zero.
solution: At a root of $D$, the system has a solution iff $\operatorname{adj}(M)\,\mathbf b=\mathbf 0$ (equivalently all $D_x,D_y,D_z$ vanish and consistent).
For each root, one left null vector $w$ of $M$ is a row of $\operatorname{adj}M$; the system is inconsistent iff $w\cdot\mathbf b\neq0$.
All three roots give no solution, so $12\sum|\lambda|=12\left(1+\frac13+\frac23\right)=24$ (the same answer).

useful_results: For a square system $M\mathbf v=\mathbf b$ with $|M|=0$: no solution iff some left null vector $w$ ($w^TM=0$) has $w^T\mathbf b\neq0$ (Fredholm alternative); otherwise infinitely many solutions.
A row of $\operatorname{adj}(M)$ (when $|M|=0$ and rank $=n-1$) is a left null vector, so $\operatorname{adj}(M)\mathbf b\neq0$ means no solution.
Instance: $9\lambda^3-7\lambda-2=(\lambda-1)(3\lambda+1)(3\lambda+2)$, and each root gives rank $2$ vs augmented rank $3$.

concepts: Properties of determinants: summing a row over $k$ (linearity)
questions.question: Let $D_k=\begin{vmatrix}1&2k&2k-1\\n&n^2+n+2&n^2\\n&n^2+n&n^2+n+2\end{vmatrix}$. If $\sum_{k=1}^{n}D_k=96$, then $n$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $k$ appears only in the first row, so $\sum D_k$ is the same determinant with that row replaced by its row-sums.
solution: $k$ occurs only in the first row, and a determinant is linear in each row, so $\sum_{k=1}^nD_k$ equals the determinant with the first row summed over $k$.
$n=6$ ($n=-8$ is rejected as $n$ is a positive integer).

alternate_solutions.idea: Expand $D_k$ itself: it is linear in $k$, so $\sum D_k$ follows from $\sum k$.
solution: Expanding along the first row: $D_k=(n^3+5n^2+4n+4)-2k\cdot n(n+2)-(2k-1)\cdot2n$.

useful_results: A determinant is linear in each row/column separately; if a parameter $k$ appears only in one row, $\sum_kD_k$ is the determinant with that row summed over $k$.
Subtracting the first row from the others often triangularises a determinant whose rows share a common part; the determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal.
Instance: $\sum_{k=1}^6D_k=2\cdot6\cdot8=96$.
